The independent test of the AGA rule in a consecutive aspiration cohort found 62% sensitivity, 79% specificity, 57% positive and 82% negative predictive value, from 13 events among 41 verified patients with no confidence intervals reported, main-duct IPMN excluded, and the criteria applied at aspiration rather than on MRI — which the authors say makes 62% an overestimate of the rule's real performance.

avoid.t: Do not offer prophylactic total pancreatectomy for a pancreatic cyst.
avoid.pref: Kyoto 2024: prophylactic total pancreatectomy is not recommended because of its endocrine and exocrine metabolic consequences, but the possibility of total pancreatectomy should be discussed with all patients before an operation that might require it. Kyoto adds that multifocality does not raise the risk of high-grade dysplasia or carcinoma, so a multifocal branch-duct IPMN is managed by its highest-risk lesion and only that lesion is resected.
avoid.avoid: The systematic review that underpins the shared-decision material found no studies at all of prophylactic total pancreatectomy — two papers mention the concept — so the 25% major morbidity, 6% 30-day mortality, 33% exocrine insufficiency, 18% endocrine-related readmission and 1.8% hypoglycaemia-related mortality are figures for total pancreatectomy for all indications pooled together, in patients mostly operated for disease rather than prophylaxis. The programme that proposes it rests on 35 patients in 7 series for the minimally invasive approach, with a reported 0% mortality whose upper 95% bound is about 10%, and quotes patients a 2 to 5% operative mortality against its own pooled 6%. The 60% lifetime risk on the other side of that decision table is the prevalence of malignancy in resected main-duct specimens, so both sides of the comparison are measured on incompatible scales.
avoid.note: An international survey of 97 experts split 41% for surveillance and 59% for intervention on the precise indication those tables encode, and 46% of those favouring intervention would do a total pancreatectomy. There is no evidence base for doing this prophylactically, only an evidence base for what it costs.

gates.name: 7 · Extent of resection and the margin
crit: Whether invasive carcinoma is suspected, because that decides oncological versus parenchyma-sparing resection
Length of main-duct involvement, and whether a total pancreatectomy is foreseeable
The possibility of total pancreatectomy discussed with the patient before the operation, whatever the plan
Intraoperative frozen section of the duct transection margin available
Lymphadenectomy planned where invasive carcinoma is suspected, omitted where it is not
gates.ask: How much pancreas comes out, and what do I do when the frozen section comes back with dysplasia at the cut edge?

standard.t: Do an oncological resection with regional lymphadenectomy where invasive carcinoma is suspected, and a parenchyma-sparing operation where it is not.
standard.pref: Kyoto 2024: radical pancreatectomy with lymph node dissection should be performed when invasive carcinoma is suspected; a branch-duct IPMN can usually be completely removed by partial pancreatectomy, and organ-preserving approaches such as middle pancreatectomy or spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy are acceptable when suspicion of invasive carcinoma is low, with minimally invasive approaches acceptable. The European guideline recommends pancreatoduodenectomy with frozen section of the margins when the whole duct is dilated, and standard oncological resection with lymphadenectomy and splenectomy for any mucinous cystic neoplasm with imaging features of high-grade dysplasia or cancer.
standard.avoid: Do not do a parenchyma-sparing operation in a patient with a high-risk stigma suggesting invasion, because it forfeits the nodes and the margin. Do not add a lymphadenectomy to an enucleation for a low-suspicion lesion either — it adds morbidity for no staging benefit in a lesion that is not expected to be invasive.
standard.note: [EXPERTISE] If the resection specimen contains invasive carcinoma, the postoperative pathway is that of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma — this is the PDAC pathway from here for staging and adjuvant therapy. Kyoto 2024 notes that chemotherapy and radiotherapy for IPMN with invasive carcinoma have not been established for lack of high-quality evidence and that most physicians use PDAC regimens; in the largest resected series, adjuvant therapy given to 35 of 84 patients with invasive IPMN (42%) did not reduce recurrence.

standard.t: Take an intraoperative frozen section of the duct transection margin, and act on it by grade.
standard.pref: Kyoto 2024 recommends intraoperative frozen section to rule out unexpected main-duct involvement at the cut margin. Normal epithelium or low-grade dysplasia at the margin: no additional resection. High-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma at the margin: additional resection recommended. The practice has usable data behind it: in 412 resected IPMNs frozen section was sent in 276 (69%), was negative in 210 (76%), low or intermediate grade in 44 (16%), high grade in 11 (4%) and invasive in 11 (4%); 15 of those 22 (68.2%) had the resection extended, 9 to total pancreatectomy; it changed the planned operation in 38 of 276 cases (13.7%) and final pathology confirmed the frozen reading in 96.3%.
standard.avoid: An absence of epithelial cells at the transection margin — a denuded duct — is explicitly not equivalent to a negative margin in Kyoto 2024, and additional resection should be considered where feasible. Do not let a 'no epithelium seen' report close the case. Sendai 2006 made the same point twenty years ago and added that negative margins do not assure absence of neoplasia, because of multifocality and skip lesions.
standard.note: The evidence on what low-grade dysplasia at the margin means is genuinely mixed and Kyoto's systematic review group concluded there were insufficient data to recommend additional resection for it. The figure most often quoted for high-grade dysplasia at the margin — a hazard ratio of 20.9 for recurrence of non-invasive IPMN, P=.03 — comes from 10 margin-positive patients and is reported without a confidence interval, so it should not be carried into practice as an effect size. The margin is nonetheless one of the recurrence predictors that replicates in direction: 25% recurrence with IPMN at the margin against 14% with a negative margin (P=.008), and earlier, at a median of 37 against 48 months.

opts.name: Parenchyma-sparing resection
opts.when: Kyoto 2024 accepts middle pancreatectomy or spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy where suspicion of invasive carcinoma is low; the European guideline accepts non-oncological or spleen-preserving resection for low-risk mucinous cystic neoplasms at GRADE 2C.
opts.pref: A localised branch-duct lesion in the neck or body of a young patient, where preserving endocrine and exocrine function over decades is worth something.
opts.avoid: Not where invasion is suspected, and not where the remnant it leaves will be impossible to surveil. Central pancreatectomy has a high pancreatic fistula rate, and in the largest resected series recurrence of non-invasive IPMN was 22% after middle pancreatectomy against 7% after pancreatoduodenectomy and 6% after distal pancreatectomy (P=.016) — a difference that could reflect the operation or the selection of patients for it, with no adjustment attempted. The trade is parenchyma for morbidity, not parenchyma for nothing.

opts.name: Standard oncological partial pancreatectomy
opts.when: The default for a lesion requiring resection where invasive carcinoma is suspected or cannot be excluded.
opts.pref: Most resections on this page. It gives the margin and the nodes, and the frozen-section protocol above applies to it.
opts.avoid: Do not choose it reflexively for a small, confidently non-invasive lesion in a young patient without discussing a parenchyma-sparing alternative.

opts.name: Total pancreatectomy
opts.when: Kyoto 2024: not recommended prophylactically, but the possibility should be discussed with all patients; and leaving high-grade dysplasia at the margin may be appropriate to avoid a total pancreatectomy, particularly in older or frail patients, and where invasive cancer is already present, since prognosis is then dictated by the invasive component. The European guideline reserves it for a distal mural nodule or familial pancreatic cancer, and advises against it where an IPMN-associated invasive carcinoma in the head will determine prognosis.
opts.pref: Diffuse main-duct involvement where a partial resection cannot clear high-grade disease, in a patient who understands and accepts an apancreatic state. Discussed before the operation, never decided for the first time on the table.
opts.avoid: Twenty-five per cent major morbidity and 6% 30-day mortality (95% CI 4 to 8%) across 52 studies and 3,570 patients, exocrine insufficiency symptoms in 33% over a median 33 months, readmission for endocrine-related morbidity in 49 of 273 (18%) over a median 38 months, hypoglycaemia-related mortality in 10 of 568 (1.8%), lifelong insulin dependence and a mean global health status of 75 on a 0 to 100 scale. There are no studies of prophylactic total pancreatectomy in main-duct or mixed IPMN at all, so this is a decision taken without comparative evidence either way, and the patient-facing decision tables built for it quote 2 to 5% operative mortality rather than the 6% their own review produced.

alt.order: Ordered from least to most extensive, which is the order in which the extent should be escalated. No trial compares these in cystic neoplasms; the order reflects the physiological cost of each operation.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item: what this programme does with high-grade dysplasia at the duct margin when the extension required is a total pancreatectomy. Kyoto 2024 recommends additional resection and, in the same document, permits leaving high-grade dysplasia at the margin to avoid a total pancreatectomy. The full text narrows that apparent contradiction without removing it: the permission is conditioned on the patient being older or frail, on invasive cancer already being present so that prognosis is set by the invasive component, and on colloid-type disease, which progresses much more slowly than tubular. What is left unresolved, and it is the case that matters, is high-grade dysplasia at the margin with no invasive component in a fit patient, where the two statements point in opposite directions and total pancreatectomy carries 6% 30-day mortality. A surgeon should not be deciding that alone at 2pm. Audit: margin grade, extent taken, 90-day morbidity and mortality, and remnant recurrence.

avoid.t: Do not accept a denuded duct margin as clear.
avoid.pref: Ask the pathologist for epithelium. Where the margin is denuded and further resection is feasible, Kyoto 2024 says it should be considered.
avoid.avoid: This is a labelling problem with a surgical consequence: a report that says no dysplasia at the margin, when it means no epithelium at the margin, closes a case that is still open.

avoid.t: Do not commit to an extent of resection that was never discussed with the patient.
avoid.pref: Kyoto 2024 requires that the possibility of total pancreatectomy be put to every patient facing a resection in which it could arise. Do that in clinic, with the morbidity and mortality numbers, and document it.
avoid.avoid: An apancreatic state decided intraoperatively without a prior conversation is a consent failure, and it is not corrected by the operation having been oncologically correct.

gates.name: 8 · Surveillance of the cyst you are not resecting
crit: A named interval schedule, chosen from one guideline and written down, not assembled case by case
The same modality each time, with MRI and MRCP preferred where available
A named owner for the recall, and a system that will actually recall
Size, main duct diameter and nodule status recorded at every visit so growth rate can be computed
A review date at which the interval itself is reassessed, not only the cyst
gates.ask: Which interval schedule are we on, and whose?

opts.name: Kyoto 2024 schedule
opts.when: Cyst under 20 mm: first follow-up at 6 months, then every 18 months if stable. 20 to under 30 mm: 6 months twice, then every 12 months if stable. 30 mm or more: every 6 months. Graded SIGN 2+, recommendation B.
opts.pref: The spine of this page, and the only one of the four with published data under its size bands: pooled progression to worrisome features was 4.8% at a median of 54 months for lesions under 10 mm, 10% at 55 months for 10 to 20 mm and 48.8% at a median of 23 months for 20 to 30 mm. Its intervals are the most generous for small cysts of any guideline that keeps surveilling them.
opts.avoid: Two limits. It is an IPMN guideline and nothing else — no schedule for mucinous cystic neoplasms, serous cystadenomas or cystic neuroendocrine tumours — so a programme adopting it still has to borrow the non-IPMN intervals from elsewhere. And its 30 mm band has validation evidence against it: in the 3,336-patient cohort that validated the rest of the criteria, long-term risk was stratified at 20 mm but not at 30 mm, the subdistribution hazard ratio being 2.07 (95% CI 1.38 to 3.10) for 20 to 29 mm and 1.75 (1.00 to 3.08) for 30 mm or more. The band that triggers the most imaging is the one that did not separate.

opts.name: ACG 2018 schedule
opts.when: Escalating with size, as published in full: under 1 cm, MRI every 2 years for 4 years; 1 to 2 cm, MRI yearly for 3 years then every 2 years for 4 years; 2 to 3 cm, MRI or EUS every 6 to 12 months for 3 years then yearly for 4 years; over 3 cm, MRI alternating with EUS every 6 months for 3 years then alternating yearly for 4 years, with multidisciplinary referral. Lengthening may be considered once stability is documented. New or worsening diabetes, or growth of more than 3 mm per year, prompts a short-interval MRI or EUS with or without aspiration.
opts.pref: The most commonly used schedule in US practice and the one most radiologists will recognise. ACG names MRCP the preferred modality and accepts EUS where MRI is unavailable.
opts.avoid: Conditional recommendation on very low quality evidence, by ACG's own grading of all 20 of its recommendations, and the guideline states that there are very little data on whether intervals can be extended and none to guide stopping by age. It also excludes from scope patients with a strong family history of pancreatic cancer or a predisposing germline mutation, which is the group in whom surveillance is most likely to be worthwhile.

opts.name: European 2018 schedule
opts.when: MRI preferred; 6-monthly in the first year, then yearly thereafter when no risk factors are present, and 6-monthly for patients with a relative indication, the elderly and those with severe comorbidity — the same for IPMN and for mucinous cystic neoplasms under 40 mm. Follow-up continues for life while the patient is fit for surgery. Graded 1B with strong agreement.
opts.pref: The simplest schedule to run and audit, because it does not branch on size, and the only one that covers the non-IPMN cysts as well. Its own rationale is that the risk of IPMN progression increases over time, with progression of branch-duct IPMN expected in about 10 to 15% over 3 to 5 years, and it asks for the whole gland to be covered because of the risk of a new cancer elsewhere.
opts.avoid: It is the most imaging-intensive of the four for a small stable cyst — yearly, indefinitely — and that cost is not matched by any demonstrated outcome advantage. The GRADE 1B label should not be read as high-quality evidence either: the single comorbidity study the guideline cites in support of lifelong follow-up reports that patients with a Charlson-age index of 7 or more have an elevenfold risk of comorbidity-related death within 3 years and that only 6% die of malignant IPMN, which argues against the recommendation it accompanies.

opts.name: AGA 2015 schedule
opts.when: For cysts under 3 cm without a solid component or a dilated duct: MRI at 1 year, then every 2 years, for a total of 5 years. EUS-FNA only when at least two of three high-risk features are present — size 3 cm or more, a dilated main duct, or an associated solid component.
opts.pref: The least intensive schedule, and the only one with an explicit endpoint. Every recommendation in it is graded conditional on very low quality evidence by the AGA itself.
opts.avoid: Do not adopt it without stating what it misses and what it is built on. The AGA says in its own text that the 1-year-then-2-year interval 'is not based on any evidence but is believed to be reasonable', that there are no data on the effect of multiple high-risk features, and that a dilated main duct was retained as a high-risk feature although its own review of unselected cysts found no significant association with malignancy. Applied to 225 consecutive patients having EUS-FNA, the criteria detected advanced neoplasia with 62% sensitivity, 79% specificity, 57% positive and 82% negative predictive value and missed 5 of 11 IPMNs harbouring adenocarcinoma or high-grade dysplasia (45%) — figures resting on 13 events among 41 verified patients, with no confidence intervals, main-duct IPMN excluded, and the criteria applied at aspiration rather than on MRI, which the authors say makes 62% an overestimate. Applied in retrospect to 75 resected suspected IPMNs, they would have avoided 21 resections (28%) but missed 4 of 33 patients (12%) with high-grade dysplasia or malignancy — effectively two lesions — against none missed by the IAP or European criteria, in a cohort those two guidelines had selected.

standard.order: Ordered with the page's declared spine first, then by how widely each is used in US practice. The order carries no claim of superiority. No trial has ever compared these four schedules against each other on any outcome; the current review of the field concludes that long-term prospective comparative studies of observation against resection are lacking and that the natural history data needed to choose between the schedules do not exist. Three of the four state in their own texts that their intervals are not evidence-based.
standard.flagnote: The central ratification item on this page. The programme must pick one schedule and write it down, because the four differ by a factor of three or more in imaging per patient-decade for the same cyst, and because a schedule assembled case by case cannot be audited, cannot generate a growth rate, and will drift. Decide also which schedule applies to mucinous cystic neoplasms and cystic neuroendocrine tumours, since Kyoto 2024 covers neither, and whether the Kyoto 30 mm band is retained now that its only large validation found no stratification at that threshold. Audit: schedule assigned at enrolment, adherence to interval, proportion of scans on the assigned modality, and progression events by schedule.

standard.t: Use MRI with MRCP as the surveillance modality wherever it is available, and keep the same modality for the life of the surveillance.
standard.pref: ACG names MRCP the preferred modality for pancreatic cyst surveillance and accepts EUS as the primary tool where MRI is unavailable; the European guideline prefers MRI at GRADE 2C for its sensitivity to duct communication, mural nodules, septations and multifocality and because repeated CT radiation carries its own risk, reserving CT for calcification, staging and postoperative recurrence; Kyoto 2024 writes its intervals as CT or MRI and reports that MDCT, MRI and EUS are equivalent for diagnosing high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma.
standard.avoid: Do not alternate modality for convenience. A size difference between a CT in one year and an MRI the next is not reliably a size difference, and growth is a worrisome feature in Kyoto 2024 at 2.5 mm per year — well inside the disagreement between two modalities. Note also that neither Kyoto nor the European guideline can recommend a specific MRI or CT protocol: the European guideline says so explicitly, for want of comparative studies.
standard.note: The cost of the commitment now has published numbers, and they are not reassuring in either direction. Up to $3.6 million is spent on cyst surveillance per cancer detected in the United States, with no appreciable change in cyst-related pancreatic adenocarcinoma mortality over two decades of rising expenditure; one Markov model of IAP 2017 surveillance against no surveillance in a 60-year-old with an asymptomatic 25 mm cyst returned an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of $171,143 per quality-adjusted life-year, while an earlier model of 2006 consensus surveillance in a 60-year-old returned $20,096 per QALY — two models differing in cyst size, guideline, era and assumptions, which the review that prints both does not reconcile. Sendai 2006, Fukuoka 2012, Fukuoka 2017, Kyoto 2024, ACG 2018 and the European 2018 guideline contain no cost analysis at all, and ACG and AGA both state that none exists. This is not a reason to under-image a patient; it is a reason for the programme to know how many scans it is committing to.

alt.t: Alternate MRI with EUS in the cyst of 2 cm or more, where the question is a mural nodule rather than size.
alt.pref: ACG brings EUS into the schedule at 2 to 3 cm; Fukuoka 2017 alternated MRI with EUS at 2 to 3 cm and every 3 to 6 months above 3 cm. EUS is the modality Kyoto names for confirming a mural nodule and measuring its height, and the 5 mm nodule threshold is the single most consequential measurement on this page.
alt.avoid: Do not add EUS to a schedule for a small stable cyst — it adds a sedated procedure to each cycle without changing the question. And do not let an EUS report that omits the nodule measurement count as an EUS.
alt.note: [EXPERTISE] Inter-operator variation in nodule measurement is not published and is not audited anywhere; a programme that makes operative decisions on a 5 mm EUS threshold should know who is measuring.

alt.t: Consider earlier resection in a young fit patient facing decades of surveillance, and say that the argument is about the duration of the commitment rather than about the cyst.
alt.pref: Fukuoka 2012 said surgery should be strongly considered in young fit patients with a cyst above 3 cm, and Fukuoka 2017 that patients under 65 with cysts over 2 cm may still be candidates. The supporting observation is that risk accumulates rather than plateaus: cumulative incidence of pancreatic carcinoma was 3.3% at 5 years, 6.6% at 10 and 15.0% at 15 in 1,404 branch-duct IPMNs, and Kyoto 2024 states that its own option to discontinue surveillance does not apply to younger patients with branch-duct IPMN, because the risk appears cumulative over time.
alt.avoid: Kyoto 2024 does not carry the early-resection recommendation forward, and no study has compared early resection against continued surveillance in young patients. Do not present it as the guideline position — it is a reasonable conversation, not a standard. Fukuoka 2017 also demoted cyst size as a surgical indication in its own text while keeping the 2 cm figure for patients under 65, so the recommendation is internally inconsistent at source.
alt.note: This argument cuts both ways. The same young patient has the most years in which to suffer the long-term consequences of a pancreatectomy, and the most years in which a remnant can produce a new lesion: after resection of 130 non-invasive IPMNs the 1-, 5- and 10-year risks of a new IPMN were 4%, 25% and 62%, with invasive IPMN in 0%, 7% and 38% by 10 years.

avoid.t: Do not run surveillance without a named owner and a recall system that fails loudly.
avoid.pref: One owner per patient, an interval recorded in the record rather than in a letter, and a report that lists overdue patients by name every month.
avoid.avoid: Every schedule on this page assumes the scan happens. A surveillance programme whose default failure mode is silent is not safer than no programme — it is a programme that carries the cost and generates the reassurance without the benefit. This is an operational requirement, grade D, and is audited for adherence rather than for effect.

avoid.t: Do not mix the four schedules, taking the generous interval from one and the stopping rule from another.
avoid.pref: Adopt one schedule whole, note the deviations deliberately, and record which version and which date.
avoid.avoid: Each of the four is internally coherent: AGA's long intervals go with its 5-year stop, the European guideline's short intervals go with lifelong follow-up, and Kyoto's 18-month interval for a small cyst goes with its conditional 5-year discontinuation option. Assembling the longest intervals with the latest stopping point produces a schedule no guideline has ever examined.

gates.name: 9 · Stopping surveillance
crit: No longer a candidate for pancreatectomy, on fitness or on the patient's own decision — the one trigger all four guidelines share
Five years of documented stability with no worrisome feature, in a cyst under the programme's stated size threshold
Age and size meeting the programme's stated age-and-size rule, where it has adopted one
Competing-risk estimate short enough that the cyst cannot become the cause of death
gates.ask: Can we stop, and on whose rule — because the three cohorts that answer this question answer it oppositely, and the reason is in how each was built?

standard.t: Stop when the patient is no longer a candidate for pancreatectomy. This is the only stopping rule all four guidelines share.
standard.pref: Every patient, reassessed at each visit rather than once at enrolment. ACG makes it a strong recommendation and adds that it is reasonable to assess the utility of ongoing surveillance in patients over 75, with an individualised approach for those aged 76 to 85 — age limits ACG says in the same paragraph are borrowed from USPSTF colorectal screening and are not supported by evidence. Kyoto 2024 adds a life expectancy under 10 years as a reason to stop.
standard.avoid: Do not treat it as an age rule. Fitness, not birthday, is the criterion, and an 80-year-old who would accept and survive a distal pancreatectomy is still a surveillance candidate.
standard.note: Grade D: this is a logical requirement, not a comparative result. No study has randomised stopping against continuing in anyone, and no cost-effectiveness analysis of surveillance in an elderly population exists.

opts.name: Continue while the patient remains fit — European 2018 and ACG 2018
opts.when: The European guideline, at GRADE 1B: 'the risk of IPMN progression increases over the time, therefore patients affected by IPMN without indication for surgery should be followed up until they are no longer fit for surgery'. ACG discontinues only on loss of surgical candidacy, with the over-75 assessment above, and explicitly rejects the AGA 5-year rule on the ground that genetic studies put the dwell time to cancer at 15 to 20 years and cancers have appeared in IPMN up to 16 years after diagnosis.
opts.pref: The position with the longest follow-up behind it. In 577 branch-duct IPMNs at one US referral centre, 363 were surveilled beyond 5 years for a median of 107 months and 20 of those (5.5%) developed high-grade dysplasia or invasive neoplasm after the 5-year mark, with invasive cancer in 16 (4.4%) and malignant transformation after 10 years in 5 of 121 (4%); the standardised incidence ratio for the 282 patients without worrisome features at 5 years was 18.8 (95% CI 9.7 to 32.8). In 1,404 branch-duct IPMNs in Tokyo, 804 were followed past 5 years for a median of 107 months with a cumulative incidence of 12.0% at 15 years from diagnosis and a standardised incidence ratio beyond 5 years of 5.8 (3.7 to 7.9); among the 737 who would have met the AGA criteria for discontinuation, 23 carcinomas occurred, with a post-5-year standardised incidence ratio of 4.8 (2.9 to 6.8).
opts.avoid: The cost is indefinite imaging in a population whose competing risk of death is far larger than their cyst risk. And both standardised incidence ratios are inflated by construction in the same two ways: each counts high-grade dysplasia as an event against a cancer-registry comparator that counts only invasive cancer — the US cohort supplies a sensitivity analysis restricted to invasive disease, giving 15.6 (7.5 to 28.7), and its abstract carries the 18.8 — and each compares a referral cohort known to harbour a pancreatic cyst against a general population of whom 2 to 7% also harbour one, so part of the excess is detection. The Tokyo authors note that their own incidence exceeds what cyst prevalence and population cancer rates would predict.

opts.name: Stop at 5 years if stable — AGA 2015, and one of Kyoto 2024's two options
opts.when: AGA 2015 recommends discontinuing surveillance if there has been no significant change in cyst characteristics after 5 years (conditional, very low quality), on a reviewed transformation risk of about 0.24% per year computed by assuming that every pancreatic cancer arises in a cyst. Kyoto 2024 offers two options for a small unchanged branch-duct IPMN after 5 years — 'stop surveillance' or 'continue surveillance for possible development of concomitant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma' — and states that surveillance may be discontinued for cysts under 20 mm with no morphological change and no worrisome feature after 5 years, with consideration of patient condition and life expectancy (SIGN 2+, grade C).
opts.pref: Small stable cysts in older patients, where the competing-risk argument dominates: among 1,617 presumed branch-duct IPMNs stable for at least 5 years, all-cause mortality was 4.9% and disease-specific mortality 0.3%.
opts.avoid: The AGA version was not restricted by size, rests on a population-level estimate with no data comparing cancer rates in stable against changing cysts — the guideline says so — and has been repeatedly criticised. Kyoto's version is explicitly conditional, size-limited to 20 mm, excluded from younger patients and from those with familial or genetic risk, and offered as one of two permissible courses, so a pathway that adopts it cannot claim evidential support for the course it chose; the guideline records that the two options exist because most Japanese physicians accept the low progression risk of a small stable lesion while remaining concerned about concomitant adenocarcinoma. Kyoto's own counterweight is a Japanese series of 732 patients with branch-duct IPMN under 15 mm in which 22 pancreatic carcinomas occurred, cumulative incidence 2.2%, 4.6% and 7.4% at 5, 10 and 15 years, 14 of the 22 being concomitant adenocarcinomas. The best estimate of what happens after an uneventful 5 years in a guideline-adherent cohort is 2.7% (1.9 to 3.7) at 10 years and 6.1% (4.3 to 8.3) at 15, from a centre that surveilled more intensively than Kyoto advises and whose authors say so.

opts.name: Stop by age and size — the standardised-incidence-ratio argument
opts.when: Not a guideline position, but the best-quantified one. In an international cohort of 3,844 presumed branch-duct IPMNs with no worrisome features or high-risk stigmata at diagnosis, 1,617 (42%) developed none in the first 5 years, and in that subgroup the standardised incidence ratio for pancreatic cancer was 2.29 (95% CI 1.22 to 3.91) overall, 1.12 (0.23 to 3.39, from 3 cancers) in patients aged 75 or older, and 0.95 (0.11 to 3.42, from 2 cancers) in patients 65 or older with stable lesions of 15 mm or less.
opts.pref: The authors' own proposal: discontinuation could be justified after 5 years of stability in patients over 75 with cysts under 30 mm, and in patients 65 or older with cysts of 15 mm or less. It gives a programme two defensible numbers rather than one blanket rule, and it is the only one of the three cohorts that excluded worrisome features by design, so it is the only one describing the lesion a stopping rule would actually be applied to.
opts.avoid: Four limits, each of which the paper states and none of which survives into the recommendation. The intervals are wide because the events are few — two and three cancers — so 'no different from the population' is a failure to exclude a threefold excess, not a demonstration of safety. The standardised incidence ratio falls with age because the comparator population's pancreatic cancer incidence rises steeply with age, which the paper says explicitly, so the rule licenses stopping in exactly the group whose absolute risk is highest. Size is not neutral within the stable group: cysts above 30 mm with no new feature for 5 years had a standardised incidence ratio of 10.29 (4.12 to 21.21). And the group this applies to cannot be identified at diagnosis — 20.2% developed a worrisome feature and 1.8% a high-risk stigma during follow-up, so this is the 42% who stayed stable, known only in retrospect.

standard.order: Ordered from the most conservative to the most permissive. No winner is picked here and none should be read in. The three cohorts differ on four things, and those four differences account for the opposite conclusions, so the order reflects how much imaging each position commits the programme to and not any comparison of outcomes. First, baseline selection: the two cohorts that found a large excess admitted cysts that already had or went on to develop worrisome features — 36% of the US cohort had worrisome features or high-risk stigmata at some point, and the Tokyo cohort counted a mural nodule developing during follow-up as an outcome (subdistribution hazard ratio 11.5, 4.49 to 29.6) — while the cohort that found no excess excluded those cysts by design at entry and again at 5 years. Second, conditioning on survival: all three report a denominator of patients who reached 5 years without being resected or diagnosed, which continuously purges the cohort of its highest-risk members in whichever direction the authors are arguing. Third, the numerator: the two high estimates count high-grade dysplasia as an event against invasive-cancer-only registry comparators, which is what produces standardised incidence ratios of 18.8 and 10.8, while the low estimate counts invasive cancer only, and 14 of its 40 cancers were diagnosed radiologically or on aspiration rather than pathologically. Fourth, observation past the mark: the two high estimates watched for a median of 107 months each beyond 5 years, the low estimate for 85. Nothing about biology separates these papers that is not also explained by how they were built.
standard.flagnote: The second central ratification item. The programme must choose a stopping rule and state it, because the three positions have different failure modes: continuing indefinitely spends imaging on patients who will die of something else, stopping at 5 years accepts a documented 4.4% rate of invasive cancer after that point in one referral cohort, and the age-and-size rule rests on two and three events with confidence intervals compatible with a threefold excess, in a cohort no guideline has endorsed. Decide also whether a patient who stops is told they may still develop a pancreatic cancer unrelated to the cyst, and whether a cyst above 30 mm is excluded from any stopping rule, since stable cysts above 30 mm carried a standardised incidence ratio of 10.29 in the cohort that proposed stopping. Audit: stopping decisions by rule applied, and any pancreatic cancer diagnosed in a patient after surveillance stopped.

alt.t: Where surveillance stops but the patient is still fit, consider stopping for the cyst while remaining alert to a concomitant adenocarcinoma elsewhere in the gland.
alt.pref: This is Kyoto 2024's second option in plain terms, and it has a mechanistic basis. Of 68 pancreatic carcinomas in 1,404 branch-duct IPMNs, 30 were concomitant ductal adenocarcinomas arising elsewhere; cyst size and duct diameter predicted the IPMN-derived cancers but not the concomitant ones, and older age was the only risk factor for a concomitant cancer. In the later 3,179-patient analysis from the same centre, 68 of 138 carcinomas were concomitant, the worrisome-feature count did not predict them, and they were metastatic at diagnosis three times as often as the derived cancers (21% against 7.1%).
alt.avoid: Kyoto 2024 puts the yearly incidence of concomitant adenocarcinoma at 0.4 to 1.0%, about 3 to 5 times the age-matched population — but adds that most of these data come from Japan, where the whole resected pancreas is sectioned at 5 mm and clinicians are primed to look for the entity, and that elsewhere the risk in an IPMN patient appears similar to the general population. Do not quote the Japanese figure to a Houston patient as their own risk.
alt.note: If the concomitant-cancer risk really is background outside Japan, the case for indefinite surveillance of a stable small cyst weakens considerably. This is the single biggest unresolved question behind the stopping debate. One related guideline position also fails to replicate: Fukuoka 2017 and Kyoto 2024 both treat a family history of pancreatic cancer as raising the risk of concomitant adenocarcinoma, and Kyoto halves the post-resection surveillance interval on it, but in the 3,179-patient Tokyo cohort a family history was not associated with carcinoma incidence, overall or by carcinoma type.

avoid.t: Do not call stopping a discharge without telling the patient what is being accepted.
avoid.pref: Say the numbers: that a cyst of this size, stable for this long, in a person of this age, carries a risk of pancreatic cancer close to that of anyone else their age; that the risk is not zero; and what symptoms should bring them back.
avoid.avoid: A letter saying 'no further follow-up required' in a disease where one referral cohort found 4.4% invasive cancers after year 5 is not an honest account of the decision, and it leaves no route back in. Say also what the number rests on: of the 64 patients in the low-risk international cohort who were eventually resected after 5 years or more, 24 (38.1%) had high-grade dysplasia or invasive cancer, so when these cysts do declare themselves they are often already advanced.

avoid.t: Do not let surveillance stop by default, through missed appointments or a lapsed recall.
avoid.pref: A stop is a decision with a date, an owner and a note. Overdue is not stopped.
avoid.avoid: The commonest way surveillance ends in practice is that nobody books the next scan. That is indistinguishable in the record from a considered decision and is not one. Operational requirement, grade D.

gates.name: 10 · After resection: the remnant
crit: Final histology, with the highest grade in the specimen and the margin status including whether the margin was denuded
Whether any residual cyst was knowingly left in the remnant, and where
Family history of pancreatic cancer established, because it changes the interval in Kyoto 2024
A surveillance schedule assigned at discharge, not at the first outpatient visit
Whether the patient remains fit for a second operation, because that is what the surveillance is for
gates.ask: What am I watching in the remnant, for how long, and what would I actually do about it?

opts.name: Kyoto 2024 — interval by risk factor
opts.when: Yearly imaging for patients without additional risk factors, and every 6 months for those with a family history of pancreatic cancer or high-grade dysplasia in the resected specimen. Continue as long as the patient remains fit to undergo additional therapeutic intervention. IPMN-specific surveillance may be stopped 5 years after a total pancreatectomy for non-invasive disease. Graded SIGN 2+, recommendation C.
opts.pref: The spine of this page, and the only one of the four that stratifies the post-resection interval on something other than the grade of the resected lesion. It is also the only one that quantifies what is being looked for: median cumulative 5-year incidence of clinically significant remnant lesions 10% (range 0 to 21%), of all remnant lesions 19% (8 to 28%) and of invasive remnant lesions 4% (1 to 10%), with the risk continuing to rise beyond 5 years.
opts.avoid: No comparative data support 6 months over 12 in either group; these are consensus intervals built on observational risk factors. One of the two factors also fails to replicate: in a 3,179-patient surveillance cohort a family history of pancreatic cancer was not associated with carcinoma incidence, overall or by type, although it was associated with concomitant adenocarcinoma in the resected series Fukuoka 2017 cites (11.1% against 2.9%, P=0.002).

opts.name: ACG 2018 — interval by grade
opts.when: All surgically resected IPMNs require postoperative surveillance (strong, very low quality). For low- or intermediate-grade dysplasia with no residual cyst, MRI every 24 months appears reasonable; for high-grade dysplasia or invasive cancer, MRI or EUS every 6 months. Resected mucinous cystic neoplasms without cancer require no postoperative surveillance (strong, low quality), as do resected serous cystadenomas and pseudocysts; solid pseudopapillary neoplasms are followed yearly for at least 5 years.
opts.pref: Simple to run, and the only one of the four that explicitly releases a resected mucinous cystic neoplasm from follow-up.
opts.avoid: ACG reports recurrence in 17 to 65% of IPMNs resected with cancer and 13 to 31% after high-grade dysplasia, at a median of 19 to 47 months and a range of 4 to 180, which are very wide bands, and 0 to 22% after low- or intermediate-grade dysplasia, for which the 24-month interval has no comparative support. ACG also states that conflicting results exist on the risk after resection of low- or intermediate-grade disease and that there is insufficient evidence to support no surveillance in that group — so its own 24-month interval is a compromise rather than a finding. The strong recommendation releasing a resected mucinous cystic neoplasm rests on a 90-patient series and a 344-case review in which no lesion under 3 cm with a normal CA 19-9 and no concerning features harboured high-grade dysplasia or cancer, which is an absence of events in modest series.

opts.name: European 2018 — lifelong, intensified for high-grade or main-duct disease
opts.when: Lifelong surveillance following resection of an IPMN as long as the patient is fit and willing to undergo surgery if indicated. IPMN with high-grade dysplasia, or main-duct IPMN, every 6 months for the first 2 years then yearly.
opts.pref: The most explicit on the condition that makes post-resection surveillance meaningful at all — that the patient would accept a second operation.
opts.avoid: The most imaging-intensive option over a lifetime, and the recommendation is a consensus position derived by GRADE from observational evidence only. Its own supporting figures: recurrence after resection is possible 5 to 10 years out and similar for branch-duct and main-duct disease at 7 to 8%, with 5.4 to 10% after low-grade dysplasia at a disease-free survival of about 52 months, against above 50% after high-grade dysplasia or an associated invasive carcinoma at a disease-free survival of 29 months.

opts.name: AGA 2015 — no routine surveillance without high-grade dysplasia or cancer
opts.when: AGA 2015 recommends against routine surveillance of pancreatic cysts without high-grade dysplasia or malignancy at surgical resection (conditional, very low quality), and MRI every 2 years after resection of a cyst with invasive cancer or dysplasia.
opts.pref: Stated here because it is the position a referring clinician may have applied, and because the page should say where it sits.
opts.avoid: It conflicts with all three of the other guidelines, which surveil every resected IPMN, and the AGA concedes that no case series report outcomes in the group it proposes to discharge. The two recommendations are also argued in opposite directions in consecutive paragraphs: post-resection imaging after dysplasia is justified on a field defect, and no surveillance after a benign resection on the inference that such patients are unlikely to have one. The best recurrence series gives 65 of 381 patients (17%) recurring at a median of 17 months, with 5- and 10-year disease-free survival of 82% and 78% and recurrence in 28 of 299 non-invasive lesions (9%) — low, but not nothing, and later than the invasive recurrences.

standard.order: Ordered with the page's spine first, then from most to least surveillance. The order carries no outcome claim: no study compares post-resection schedules, and the recurrence data below are from a single-centre retrospective series with near-complete follow-up.
standard.flagnote: Ratification item: the post-resection schedule, and specifically whether a resected non-invasive branch-duct IPMN with a clear margin is surveilled at all. Three guidelines say yes and AGA says no, and the best recurrence series suggests the honest answer is 'rarely but not never, and later than you expect'. Decide also whether a resected mucinous cystic neoplasm without cancer is followed, where ACG says no and the European guideline is silent. Audit: post-resection schedule assigned by histology, remnant recurrence, and reoperation.

standard.t: Base the schedule on the recurrence pattern, which depends on invasion, on the margin and on subtype, not on the fact of having had an operation.
standard.pref: In 412 resected IPMNs with near-complete follow-up at one centre, 65 of 381 (17%) recurred over a median of 58 months and 5- and 10-year disease-free survival were 82% and 78%. Invasive IPMN recurred in 37 of 82 (45%) against 28 of 299 (9%) for non-invasive disease (P<.001) and much earlier, at a median of 19 against 52 months; IPMN at the resection margin gave 25% recurrence (15 of 59) against 14% (42 of 301) with a negative margin (P=.008). In non-invasive disease, high-grade dysplasia at the margin independently predicted recurrence (hazard ratio 20.9, P=.03) while low- or intermediate-grade dysplasia did not; in invasive disease the tubular subtype was the independent predictor (hazard ratio 2.7 over colloid, P=.02).
standard.avoid: Those two hazard ratios come from 10 margin-positive patients and 84 invasive cases respectively and are reported without confidence intervals, so use them for direction and not as effect sizes. Recurrence here means the radiologic appearance of a new IPMN, with growth of lesions knowingly left behind excluded by definition and most recurrences never histologically confirmed, so the distinction between true recurrence, progression of residual disease and a field defect is settled by the definition rather than by evidence. Follow-up intensity also differed by design between the groups — 6-monthly for 3 years after invasive IPMN against yearly then 2- to 3-yearly after non-invasive — so the later median recurrence of benign lesions is partly a detection interval. Only 2 patients (0.5%) developed a metachronous ductal adenocarcinoma, but 19 patients with a concomitant adenocarcinoma were excluded from the recurrence analysis beforehand, so this series cannot be used to estimate the risk of a new cancer elsewhere in the remnant, which is the risk post-resection surveillance is usually justified by.
standard.note: The authors' own conclusion was that recurrence of non-invasive branch-duct IPMN is infrequent — 1 of 197 (0.5%) recurred as a malignant tumour, which is a single patient — and that surveillance may be avoided in selected cases. Set against that, Fukuoka 2017 cites a series in which the 1-, 5- and 10-year risks of a new IPMN after resection of 130 non-invasive lesions were 4%, 25% and 62%, with further surgery needed in 1.6%, 14% and 18% and invasive IPMN developing in 0%, 7% and 38%, and the wider literature it reviews gives 1 to 20% recurrence and 2 to 7.8% invasive recurrence. Late events are real: in the 412-patient series 4 of the 5 patients reoperated beyond 4 years had an oncocytic lesion, one recurring 11 years after the original resection. This page records the disagreement rather than resolving it.

alt.t: Where a residual branch-duct cyst was knowingly left in the remnant, record exactly where it is and surveil it as a cyst in its own right.
alt.pref: A multifocal branch-duct IPMN in which a total pancreatectomy was rightly declined — Kyoto 2024 states that multifocality does not raise the risk of high-grade dysplasia or carcinoma and that only the highest-risk lesion should be resected. In the 412-patient series a residual branch-duct IPMN of a median 10 mm was left in the remnant in 33 patients (9%); over a median of 61 months these grew to a median of 13 mm, none developed worrisome features or high-risk stigmata, and none required reoperation.
alt.avoid: Do not let the residual cyst disappear from the record between the operation note and the surveillance plan. Kyoto 2024's remnant surveillance applies for as long as the patient is fit for further intervention, which means the plan has to name what is being watched.
alt.note: Thirty-three patients with no progression is reassuring and is also a small number over a median follow-up of 5 years, in a series whose own authors say they cannot rule out that the retained lesions harboured high-grade dysplasia. It is not a basis for discharging a remnant cyst.

alt.t: Take a family history of pancreatic cancer after the operation if it was not taken before, because in Kyoto 2024 it halves the remnant surveillance interval.
alt.pref: Every patient at the first postoperative visit. Kyoto 2024 names a family history of pancreatic cancer — defined as pancreatic cancer in one or more first-degree relatives, per the CAPS group — and high-grade dysplasia in the initial specimen as the two factors that increase the risk of a remnant lesion, and recommends 6-monthly rather than yearly imaging in either case. Fukuoka 2017 reports the supporting data: 23% recurrence against 7% with a family history (P<0.05), the only independent preoperative predictor (odds ratio 4.2, 95% CI 1.3 to 14.1), and concomitant adenocarcinoma in 11.1% against 2.9% of 324 resected cases.
alt.avoid: There are no comparative data behind the 6-month figure, and the risk factor does not replicate in surveillance: in a 3,179-patient cohort a family history was not associated with pancreatic carcinoma incidence, overall or by carcinoma type. Kyoto also states that a family history raises the incidence of concomitant adenocarcinoma without increasing the risk that the IPMN itself progresses from low-grade dysplasia. A family history may open a hereditary-risk discussion that is wider than this page and belongs with genetics, where germline ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2, MLH1 or CDKN2A mutations define a different population.
alt.note: Grade D: consensus interval on an observational risk factor that one large cohort could not reproduce.

avoid.t: Do not discharge a patient after resection of a non-invasive IPMN on the AGA rule without saying that the other three guidelines disagree.
avoid.pref: If the programme adopts the AGA position, write it down as a deliberate departure from Kyoto, ACG and the European guideline, and audit the remnant recurrences it produces.
avoid.avoid: AGA 2015 recommends against routine surveillance of resected cysts without high-grade dysplasia or malignancy; Kyoto 2024, ACG 2018 and the European guideline all surveil every resected IPMN. A patient discharged under one guideline and recalled under another has been managed inconsistently, not flexibly.

avoid.t: Do not surveil a resected serous cystadenoma or a drained pseudocyst.
avoid.pref: ACG states that resected serous cystadenomas and pseudocysts require no follow-up. Close the episode and say so in the letter.
avoid.avoid: Leaving these on a surveillance list is the clearest avoidable waste in the whole pathway: in 2,622 patients the entire international serous cystadenoma series produced three serous cystadenocarcinomas and one disease-related death.

Kyoto states that high-risk stigmata do not have perfect specificity and that the operative decision must also weigh condition, comorbidity, life expectancy and preference — without stating anywhere what the operation costs.

The schedules differ by a factor of three or more in imaging per patient-decade for the same cyst, and the stopping rules differ by the whole remainder of a life. The three cohorts behind the stopping debate reach opposite conclusions, and four structural differences account for it. Baseline selection: the two that found a large excess admitted cysts that already had or developed worrisome features — 36% of the 577-patient US cohort at some point, and a mural nodule developing during follow-up carried a hazard ratio of 11.5 in the Tokyo cohort — while the 3,844-patient international cohort excluded them at entry and again at 5 years. Numerator: the two high estimates count high-grade dysplasia as an event against invasive-cancer-only registry comparators, which is what gives standardised incidence ratios of 18.8 (9.7–32.8) and 10.8 (8.2–13.3), and the first drops to 15.6 (7.5–28.7) when restricted to invasive disease; the low estimate counts invasive cancer only and 14 of its 40 cancers were radiologic or aspiration diagnoses rather than pathological. Observation past the mark: 107 months and 107 months against 85. In the low-estimate cohort the standardised incidence ratio after 5 years of stability was 1.12 (0.23–3.39) in patients 75 or older and 0.95 (0.11–3.42) in those 65 or older with lesions of 15 mm or less — from 3 and 2 cancers — while stable cysts above 30 mm carried 10.29 (4.12–21.21), and the ratio falls with age because the comparator population's incidence rises, so the rule licenses stopping in the group at highest absolute risk. Competing risk runs the other way: all-cause mortality in that stable group was 4.9% against a disease-specific mortality of 0.3%. Kyoto 2024 covers IPMN only and supplies no interval for mucinous cystic neoplasms, serous cystadenomas or cystic neuroendocrine tumours.
