honest.t: Kyoto 2024 is the spine of this page because someone chose it, not because it has been shown to be the best of the four.
honest.why: It is the most recent, it is the only one built on systematic reviews commissioned question by question, and NCCN cites it as the international standard — but no study compares management under Kyoto against management under ACG, AGA or the European guideline on any outcome. The choice is defensible and it is still a choice; the page's job is to show what the other three would have done instead. The full-text read also showed that Kyoto's authors say of their own document that most studies on IPMN do not provide high-level evidence, and that eleven of them overlap substantially with the 2012 and 2017 working groups whose criteria they were revising, with no conflict-of-interest statement in the text.

honest.t: The malignancy percentages everyone quotes for main-duct and branch-duct IPMN — 62% and 31% — are rates in resected specimens, and Kyoto 2024 now says so itself without replacing them.
honest.why: Kyoto reports them as resected-series means with ranges of 36 to 100% and 15 to 48%, which is itself a warning, and adds in the same paragraph that given the large number of unresected indolent branch-duct lesions the real rate across all branch-duct IPMNs is much lower. It does not say how much lower, and supplies no denominator, so the risk framework of the current guideline is still calibrated on operated specimens by the guideline's own account. In surveillance cohorts the numbers are an order of magnitude smaller: 3.3% cumulative incidence of pancreatic carcinoma at 5 years in 1,404 branch-duct IPMNs. Quoting the resected figure in clinic systematically overstates the risk to the patient in front of you, and this page must not present either figure as a surveillance risk.

honest.t: Kyoto 2024 retained the 5 mm mural nodule and 10 mm main-duct thresholds against the evidence it had commissioned to examine them.
honest.why: The same document reports that a mural nodule of 5 mm or more carries an odds ratio of only 1.19 to 3.16 in the newest multivariable models and a duct of 10 mm or more 1.06 to 1.76, and that in one EUS analysis a nodule height of 10 mm gave an odds ratio of 7.90 with a 67% probability of high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma against 2.93 and under 19% for a nodule of 5 to 10 mm. It records that revising the nodule threshold to 10 mm was discussed and rejected 'for lack of evidence strongly supporting these revisions' — which places the burden of proof on change rather than on the status quo and preserves criteria that the cited evidence undercuts. The 5 mm line was itself chosen by expert agreement in 2017 after Fukuoka reported that 5, 7 and 10 mm all performed similarly. A nodule threshold separates an operation from an interval scan, so this is the most consequential unexamined number on the page.

honest.t: The 2.5 mm per year growth threshold was chosen by how often it had been published, not by how well it performed.
honest.why: Kyoto 2024 states that reported predictive growth rates range from 0.96 to 3.5 mm per year and that 2.5 mm per year was 'reported most frequently', and adopts it on that basis. The resulting variable does perform in one cohort — subdistribution hazard ratio 3.83 (95% CI 2.14 to 6.86) — but a threshold selected by vote frequency among candidate values is a grade D derivation however good the hazard ratio looks afterwards. There are now four definitions in play, not three: Kyoto 2.5 mm per year, ACG more than 3 mm per year, Fukuoka 2017 5 mm over 2 years and the European guideline 5 mm per year. None has published measurement reproducibility, and the AGA technical review found that an increase in cyst size was not a statistically significant risk factor for malignancy at all.

honest.t: Duct growth predicted later cancer where cyst growth did not, and no guideline uses it.
honest.why: In the 804 Tokyo patients followed beyond 5 years, the increase in main pancreatic duct diameter over the first 5 years predicted subsequent carcinoma (subdistribution hazard ratio 1.71 per mm, 1.44 to 2.03) while the increase in cyst size did not (1.46, 0.96 to 2.20). Kyoto 2024 considered adding 'increase in size of MPD' as a worrisome feature and rejected it for lack of evidence on this dynamic question. The median duct increase over 5 years in that cohort was 0.2 mm, so this demands a consistent measurement protocol — which is an argument for recording it, not for ignoring it.

honest.t: Three guideline generations in, there is no sensitivity, specificity or predictive value for any risk tier on this page.
honest.why: Sendai 2006, Fukuoka 2012, Fukuoka 2017 and Kyoto 2024 all report malignancy prevalences in resected series and none reports operating characteristics for high-risk stigmata or worrisome features as a classification. Fukuoka 2012's own critique of itself is that its two tiers were assembled from univariate associations in surgical series with no multivariable model and no validation cohort; Fukuoka 2017 added features without them; Kyoto 2024 gives none. The one large validation study computes them and puts them in supplementary tables, reporting only relative hazards in its main text. A clinician therefore cannot read off what a worrisome feature rules in or out — only how much more likely something is than something else.

honest.t: Surgical mortality and cost-effectiveness appear nowhere in the guidelines that set the resection thresholds.
honest.why: Sendai 2006, Fukuoka 2012, Fukuoka 2017, Kyoto 2024 and the European 2018 guideline quantify surgical mortality and morbidity nowhere in their texts, and none attempts a cost analysis — even though Kyoto invokes health economics as a reason to consider stopping surveillance and frames the whole discontinuation question around it. Every resection recommendation in the spine of this page is therefore presented one-sidedly: the risk of not operating in numbers, the risk of operating not stated. The numbers had to be assembled from elsewhere, and they are on the fourth quick-reference table. ACG and AGA are the exceptions and both state that no cost-effectiveness analysis of cyst surveillance exists.

honest.t: Counting worrisome features and acting on the count is reasonable and is not a validated decision rule.
honest.why: The additive effect is real — subdistribution hazard ratios of 1.43, 2.17 and 10.1 for one, two and three or four features in a 3,336-patient cohort — but Kyoto 2024 declines to endorse a nomogram, noting that the published ones often fail to distinguish branch-duct from main-duct disease, rest on small resected numbers in some regions and lack external validation. Its cited source for additivity reports 22%, 34%, 59% and 100% risk with one, two, three and four or more features, with no sample sizes and no confidence intervals. The gradient was also measured in a cohort purged of every patient with a high-risk stigma, and it holds only for IPMN-derived carcinoma, which was half the events. So the count tells you how hard to look; anyone who converts it into an operating threshold has invented that threshold.

honest.t: The 30 mm size tier of Kyoto's surveillance schedule has validation evidence against it, not merely absent evidence for it.
honest.why: In the only large cohort to test the revised criteria, long-term risk was stratified at 20 mm but not at 30 mm: the subdistribution hazard ratio was 2.07 (1.38 to 3.10) for a cyst of 20 to 29 mm and 1.75 (1.00 to 3.08) for 30 mm or more. The authors attribute this to an unvalidated cut-off; it is also a failure of a criterion the study set out to validate, and 30 mm is the line that triggers Kyoto's most intensive schedule and sits in every guideline's feature list in some form — 30 mm for Sendai, Fukuoka and ACG, 40 mm for the European guideline. A programme adopting a three-tier size schedule should know that the top tier is the one that did not separate.

honest.t: Kyoto's import of EUS-FNA cytology into the risk tiers creates an asymmetry it never states.
honest.why: A suspicious or positive cytology is now a high-risk stigma, and Kyoto puts the absolute risk of high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma at 91 to 100% and 100% for those two results — so a positive result is close to an absolute surgical indication. The same document puts the overall sensitivity of cyst fluid cytology at 28.7%, with a range across studies of 4.8 to 61.5%, and says that EUS cannot be delivered to the same standard everywhere and that its diagnostic ability is highly operator-dependent. A test that is decisive when positive and nearly uninformative when negative is usable, but only if everybody knows which half they are holding, and if somebody owns the question of who reads the slide.

honest.t: Roughly one cyst in four is not the entity it was called before the operation, and the page's whole structure assumes the classification is right.
honest.why: In 115 consecutive resections the preoperative diagnosis was correct in 83 (72%) and the benign-versus-premalignant distinction in 99 (86%), and accuracy was not uniform: 89% for main-duct or mixed IPMN and 80% for side-branch IPMN, but 33% for serous cystic neoplasm, 33% for neuroendocrine tumour and 50% for solid pseudopapillary neoplasm. Published accuracy for naming a cyst type is 40 to 50% in ACG's review and 40 to 95% in the European guideline's. Every interval schedule, resection threshold and stopping rule on this page is indexed to a cyst type that is wrong a substantial fraction of the time, the guidelines describe this circularity in their imaging sections and none carries it into their recommendations, and it is not fixable with current imaging. It should be said to patients.

honest.t: Cyst fluid molecular testing performs well in the hands that developed it and has not been reproduced independently at that performance.
honest.why: The prospective study is good work — 31 institutions, 1,887 adequate specimens of 1,933 — but surgical pathology existed for only 251 of 1,832 tested patients (14%), the decision to operate was itself informed by the molecular result, the allele-frequency rules that lift specificity to 98 to 100% were derived in the same group's earlier cohorts, and every specimen was analysed in the one lead laboratory, so 'multi-institutional' describes where the fluid came from. The comparison that found the AGA and IAP algorithms inferior reconstructed those guidelines retrospectively from records submitted by 31 sites with unstandardised EUS and local cytology while the panel ran prospectively in one accredited laboratory, which is not a like-for-like test. Kyoto 2024's own pooled figures for the same grade markers are far weaker — 9 to 39% sensitivity — and that gap has not been explained. The sensitivity for mucinous cystic neoplasm specifically is 47%, not 90%.

honest.t: Every cut-off this page uses from a cyst fluid test was fitted in the data that report its performance.
honest.why: CEA at 192 ng/mL was selected to maximise classification in the same 112 resected cysts in which it was then scored, of 341 enrolled, with verification driven by the findings under test. Amylase at 250 U/L and CEA at 800 ng/mL were chosen the same way in a pooled analysis that read individual values off published scatter grams and excluded IPMN entirely. The glucose meta-analyses pool cut-offs of 30, 41 and 50 mg/dL into one estimate while stating that the ideal threshold is unknown, and draw on largely the same seven primary studies, so they are not independent of each other. The molecular allele-frequency rules were tuned in the developers' own earlier cases. The 1.5 cm low-risk cyst threshold from the US surveillance cohort was derived by running a receiver-operating curve on the outcome being predicted in the same 363 patients. None of this makes the tests useless; it means none of these thresholds has been validated anywhere else.

honest.t: The three stopping papers reach opposite conclusions, and four structural differences account for all of it.
honest.why: Baseline selection: the two cohorts that found a large excess admitted cysts that already had, or went on to develop, worrisome features — 36% of the 577-patient US referral cohort had worrisome features or high-risk stigmata at some point, and in the 1,404-patient Tokyo cohort a mural nodule developing during follow-up carried a subdistribution hazard ratio of 11.5 — while the 3,844-patient international cohort excluded those cysts at entry by design and again at 5 years. Conditioning on survival: all three report a denominator of patients who reached 5 years without being resected or diagnosed (363 of 577, 804 of 1,404, 1,617 of 3,844), which continuously purges each cohort of its highest-risk members in whichever direction its authors are arguing. The numerator: the two high estimates count high-grade dysplasia as an event against cancer-registry comparators that count only invasive cancer, which is what produces standardised incidence ratios of 18.8 and 10.8 — the US figure falls to 15.6 when restricted to invasive disease, and its abstract carries 18.8 — while the low estimate counts invasive cancer only, and 14 of its 40 cancers were diagnosed radiologically or on aspiration rather than pathologically. Observation past the mark: the two high estimates watched for a median of 107 months each beyond 5 years; the low estimate watched for 85. Nothing about biology separates these three papers that is not also explained by how each was built, and a programme choosing between them is choosing a study design, not a fact.

honest.t: The argument for stopping gets stronger with age only because the comparator gets worse.
honest.why: In the international cohort the standardised incidence ratio in patients whose cyst had been stable for 5 years fell from 7.02 (2.26 to 16.38) under 65, to 2.17 (0.70 to 5.07) at 65 to 74, to 1.12 (0.23 to 3.39) at 75 or over. The paper states the mechanism explicitly: the ratio falls because the age-matched population's pancreatic cancer incidence rises steeply, not because older patients with cysts are safer. So 'a risk no different from the general population' licenses discontinuation precisely in the group whose absolute risk is highest. The competing-risk argument for stopping in that group is strong and separate — 4.9% all-cause against 0.3% disease-specific mortality — and it should be the argument the programme makes, because it is the one the data support.

honest.t: The reassuring standardised incidence ratios rest on two and three cancers.
honest.why: The subgroups that underpin the age-and-size stopping proposal produced 3 cancers in patients 75 or over (standardised incidence ratio 1.12, 0.23 to 3.39) and 2 in patients 65 or over with lesions of 15 mm or less (0.95, 0.11 to 3.42). Intervals of that width are a failure to exclude a threefold excess, not a demonstration of safety. Ascertainment also ran in the direction that favours the conclusion: 14 of the 40 cancers in the whole cohort were radiologic or aspiration diagnoses, patients lost to follow-up across 12 centres in 8 countries are nowhere accounted for, and unascertained cancers lower the numerator. And size is not neutral inside the stable group: cysts above 30 mm with no new feature for 5 years carried a standardised incidence ratio of 10.29 (4.12 to 21.21).

honest.t: Every stopping rule on this page is a competing-risk and cost judgement presented in the grammar of evidence.
honest.why: The data genuinely support both sides. Risk does not plateau — 4.4% invasive cancers after year 5 in one referral cohort, cumulative incidence reaching 15.0% at 15 years in another, 2.7% at 10 years and 6.1% at 15 after an uneventful 5 years in a third — and competing risk dominates, with 4.9% all-cause against 0.3% disease-specific mortality in patients stable for 5 years. Which number governs is a judgement about whose life-years are being spent. The one review that names this openly calls it a population-versus-individual trade-off and then conducts the argument without quantities on either side: no estimate of how many cancers a stopping rule would miss, none of how many operations and scans indefinite surveillance would add.

honest.t: If the concomitant-adenocarcinoma risk is really background outside Japan, a large part of the case for indefinite surveillance of a small stable cyst disappears.
honest.why: Kyoto 2024 puts the yearly incidence at 0.4 to 1.0%, about 3 to 5 times the age-matched population, and then says most of these data come from Japan, where the whole resected pancreas is sectioned at 5 mm and clinicians are primed to look for the entity, and that elsewhere the risk appears similar to the general population. Thirty of 68 carcinomas in the Tokyo cohort were concomitant, and 68 of 138 in the later analysis from the same centre; cyst size and duct diameter predicted the IPMN-derived cancers but not those, the worrisome-feature count does not predict them, and they are metastatic at diagnosis three times as often. Fukuoka 2017 rejected the AGA stopping rule largely on these Japanese figures while conceding in the same document that the Japanese protocol is unlikely to be applicable globally. Nobody has resolved this, and it is the biggest unanswered question behind the stopping debate.

honest.t: The family history that halves the post-resection interval did not predict cancer in the one large cohort that tested it.
honest.why: Kyoto 2024 names a family history of pancreatic cancer as one of two factors that raise the risk of a remnant lesion and recommends 6-monthly rather than yearly imaging on it, and Fukuoka 2017 supplies the supporting figures from resected series — 23% against 7% recurrence, concomitant adenocarcinoma in 11.1% against 2.9%. In a 3,179-patient surveillance cohort a family history was not associated with pancreatic carcinoma incidence, overall or by carcinoma type. Kyoto itself says a family history raises the incidence of concomitant adenocarcinoma without accelerating progression of the IPMN. The recommendation is not unreasonable; it is a grade D consensus interval on a risk factor that does not replicate, and the page should say so before it generates an extra scan every year for life.

honest.t: Kyoto 2024's two statements about high-grade dysplasia at the duct margin do not add up to a rule, although the full text narrows the gap.
honest.why: The same document recommends additional resection for high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma at the frozen-section margin, and states that leaving high-grade dysplasia there may be appropriate. The full text attaches conditions to the second statement that the recommendation summary does not: it is offered for older or frail patients, where invasive cancer is already present so that prognosis is set by the invasive component, and for colloid-type disease, which progresses much more slowly than tubular. What remains genuinely unresolved is high-grade dysplasia at the margin with no invasive component in a fit patient, where the two statements point in opposite directions and clearing it may mean a total pancreatectomy at 6% 30-day mortality. Kyoto's own systematic review group also concluded that the data on low-grade dysplasia at the margin are too mixed to recommend additional resection. This programme should decide which way it goes, in advance, with the total-pancreatectomy numbers in hand.

honest.t: There is no evidence base for prophylactic total pancreatectomy, only an evidence base for what it costs.
honest.why: The systematic review that underpins the only published shared-decision programme found no studies of prophylactic total pancreatectomy at all — two papers mention the concept. Its outcome figures pool indications, so 25% major morbidity and 6% 30-day mortality (95% CI 4 to 8%) across 3,570 patients describe total pancreatectomy for cancer and pancreatitis as well as for prophylaxis, in patients who will tolerate complications differently from a well person. The minimally invasive approach the programme is built on rests on 35 patients in 7 series with a reported 0% mortality whose upper 95% bound is about 10%. The decision tables quote patients 2 to 5% operative mortality against the review's own 6%, and put a 60% lifetime cancer risk on the other side of the comparison — a resected-specimen prevalence. An international survey of 97 experts split 41% to 59% on the same indication.

honest.t: The guideline-comparison studies cannot measure what each guideline misses in the patients nobody operated on.
honest.why: The most-quoted comparison applied three guidelines retrospectively to 115 patients who had all been resected, under the IAP and European criteria. Those two therefore determined who entered the denominator and cannot be shown to miss anything, while the AGA criteria are scored on a population they never selected — the structure of the study produces its headline result. Its '12% missed' is 4 patients and effectively two lesions counted twice. The independent test of the AGA rule in a consecutive aspiration cohort is better designed but rests on 13 events in 41 verified patients with no confidence intervals, excluded main-duct IPMN, applied the criteria at aspiration rather than on MRI — which its authors say makes the 62% sensitivity an overestimate — and compared the AGA rule against an alternative algorithm fitted in those same 41 cases. Both studies are worth reading and neither establishes a sensitivity for any guideline.

honest.t: This programme does not know what proportion of its own cyst resections removed something that needed removing.
honest.why: The published benchmark is 45% justified in retrospect in 115 consecutive resections at one centre, in an operation with real mortality — and that composite counted any neuroendocrine tumour, any solid pseudopapillary neoplasm and any symptom improvement as justification, none of which is a guideline endpoint, so the true guideline-relevant figure is lower. In the same cohort 22 patients (19.1%) had died at a median of 15 months after surgery, unrelated in the analysis to pathology or indication. A programme without its own figure is assuming it is better than published. The audit is simple — final histology against the indication recorded at the board — and until it exists the resection thresholds on this page are being applied without feedback.

honest.t: Nobody had costed what these schedules commit this system to, and now that someone has, the numbers are hard to use.
honest.why: Population MRCP finds a cyst in roughly half of middle-aged adults, with a further weighted 12.9% five-year incidence of new cysts, and the four schedules differ by a factor of three or more in imaging per patient-decade. Up to $3.6 million is spent on cyst surveillance per cancer detected in the United States, with no appreciable change in cyst-related pancreatic adenocarcinoma mortality across two decades of rising expenditure. One Markov model returns $171,143 per quality-adjusted life-year for IAP 2017 surveillance of a 25 mm cyst in a 60-year-old; an earlier one returns $20,096 per QALY for 2006 consensus surveillance; the review that prints both does not reconcile them, and they differ in cyst size, guideline, era and assumptions. A schedule the programme cannot deliver will fail silently through missed recalls, which is worse than a less ambitious schedule it can deliver.

honest.t: The population prevalence figure that frames this whole problem is a weighted estimate of lesions no guideline manages.
honest.why: The 49.1% prevalence on population MRCP is reweighted for dropout; the observed proportion was 494 of 1,077 (45.9%), the MRI response rate was 54.7% within a cohort already attrited from 4,310 to 2,333 over ten years, and the threshold counted any T2-hyperintense focus of 2 mm or more, which the authors concede is probably often dysontogenetic. Of 494 carriers, 26 (5.3%) had a largest cyst above 10 mm and 3 (0.7%) above 20 mm. The reassurance that no cyst carrier died of pancreatic disease rests on zero events over a mean 5.9 years in a lesion whose dwell time is estimated at 15 to 20 years, and two of the three SHIP participants who did die of pancreatic cancer had declined the MRI. The study establishes that small cysts are extremely common. It does not establish that they are harmless.

honest.t: The non-IPMN half of this page rests on two guidelines and one retrospective cohort each.
honest.why: Kyoto 2024 is an IPMN guideline: mucinous cystic neoplasm has been outside its scope since Fukuoka 2017 removed it on the stated ground that controversy had subsided rather than that evidence had settled anything, which left the 2012 recommendation to resect all mucinous cystic neoplasms in force unexamined. The serous cystadenoma position rests on one multinational retrospective series in which 61% of the cohort was resected, 30% of diagnoses were radiological only in a disease where blinded imaging accuracy has been reported as low as 27%, operative mortality was self-reported and the authors say probably underestimated, and the two mortality figures used to argue for conservatism have different and non-exchangeable denominators. The solid pseudopapillary position rests on no cohort at all. Those recommendations stand; they carry grade C at best and should not be quoted with the confidence of the IPMN thresholds.

honest.t: A frequently cited 2024 review tabulates branch-duct transformation rates that cannot be compared, and this page does not use it for that purpose.
honest.why: Its table places five long-term series in a single column of transformation rates reading 3.5 to 5.5%, as though they agreed across countries and designs. They do not measure the same thing: one numerator is restricted to patients already observed beyond 5 years, another is a competing-risk estimate in a five-year survivor subset, and a third is a non-operative cohort selected for having worrisome features. The apparent agreement is an artefact of tabulating incompatible denominators, and a page citing it for a transformation rate is citing that artefact. Its guideline-comparison table also reproduces several criteria inaccurately. This page cites the review for its cost figures, its account of the population-versus-individual framing and its list of circumstances in which stopping is uncontroversial, and takes every criterion and every rate from the source documents instead.

honest.t: Two of the three features in the AGA algorithm, and the rule that combines them, were adopted against or in the absence of the guideline's own evidence.
honest.why: AGA 2015 states that its own review of unselected cysts found no statistically significant association between a dilated main pancreatic duct and malignancy, and retained the duct as one of three high-risk features on the strength of resected IPMN series — the selection-biased reasoning the document criticises elsewhere. It states that there are no data on the impact of multiple high-risk features and asserts additivity by analogy with other areas of medicine, estimating the specificity of its two-feature surgical rule as likely above 95%; measured, it was 79%, with 45% of IPMNs harbouring high-grade dysplasia or cancer missed. And it says of its own surveillance interval that it 'is not based on any evidence'. The AGA position is on this page because referring clinicians apply it, and because its 5-year endpoint is a live option; it is not on this page as a derived rule.

honest.t: This is a first-draft page with no ratified institutional document behind it, and the full-text read made that more important rather than less.
honest.why: Every other roadmap in this programme transcribes an approved local protocol. There is no local pancreatic cyst protocol in the source set, so this page takes no institutional position: where the four guidelines disagree, which on this disease is on almost everything that matters, it shows the disagreement and refers the choice to the ratification items. The full-text read did not narrow those disagreements — it widened several, added a fourth growth definition, showed one Kyoto size tier contradicted by its own validation, and showed that the surgical risk the thresholds are weighed against is absent from the spine. Nineteen ratification items is not a failure of the page; it is what the evidence base actually leaves open.

board: Submission — an Epic form captures cyst size and location, main pancreatic duct diameter in millimetres, duct communication, mural nodule presence and height, modality and date of the index study and of any comparison study, symptoms, pancreatitis history, family history of pancreatic cancer, serum CA 19-9, and the specific question being asked. A submission without a duct diameter is returned. Owner: submitting clinician.

Triage — a coordinator and a clinically trained gatekeeper separate the three streams this disease generates: a new incidental cyst needing classification, a surveilled cyst with a new feature, and a resection decision. The first stream is high volume and low urgency and should not displace the third. Owners: coordinator and chair.

Agenda — stable at least 24 hours ahead. New incidental cysts without worrisome features may be handled in a batched radiology-plus-surgeon review rather than at the full board, provided the subtype, interval and owner are recorded the same way. Owner: coordinator.
Urgent lane — a same-week slot with chair approval, for jaundice with a head cyst, cyst-related acute pancreatitis, or a new solid component. Owner: chair.

Attendance — hepatopancreatobiliary surgery, advanced endoscopy, diagnostic radiology with a pancreas reader, pathology including cytopathology, gastroenterology and coordination are required for any resection decision. Medical oncology attends only where invasive carcinoma is suspected or proved. Owners: specialty leads.

Imaging — the index study reviewed by a pancreas radiologist before any recommendation, with duct diameter, nodule height and enhancement, and comparison against the prior study on the same modality, stated out loud. Owner: diagnostic radiology.

Pathology — cytopathology pre-alerted for every planned aspiration, with the fluid allocation between chemistry, cytology and molecular testing agreed before the procedure rather than in the room. Owner: pathology.

Output — one subtype, one interval, one modality, one named owner, one recall date, and the guideline schedule being applied by name and version. For a resection decision, the extent planned and whether total pancreatectomy has been discussed with the patient. Owner: chair.
Documentation — an Epic note within one business day, in the agreed structured format, with the interval and modality in a field a recall report can read rather than in prose. Owner: named owner.

Registry — every cyst entered at first presentation with subtype, size, duct diameter, schedule assigned and owner; closed on resection, on a recorded decision to stop, or on death. A cyst that is neither under surveillance nor formally stopped is a registry defect. Owner: coordinator.

Referring relationships — the referring clinician receives the subtype, the schedule by name, the interval, and who owns the recall, so that community-followed patients are followed to the same standard. The pathway returns patients with a plan; it does not capture them. Owner: named owner.
dashboard: Cysts under active surveillance, by subtype and size band, with the schedule assigned to each.
Recall adherence: proportion of surveillance scans performed within the assigned interval, and the number of patients overdue by more than 50% of their interval, reported monthly by name.
Modality consistency: proportion of surveillance studies performed on the modality the patient was enrolled on.

Report completeness: proportion of pancreatic cyst reports stating main pancreatic duct diameter in millimetres, mural nodule presence, height and enhancement, and comparison with the prior study on the same modality.
Growth events: proportion of declared growth events computed from a same-modality comparison, and whether duct diameter change was recorded alongside cyst diameter change.

Resections for cystic neoplasm: volume, 90-day mortality, major morbidity, and the proportion in which the operation was justified in retrospect by final histology or symptom relief — against the published 45% benchmark, recorded with the benchmark's composite definition stated.

Preoperative diagnostic accuracy: final histological entity against the subtype recorded at the board, against the published 72% overall and the much lower figures for serous, neuroendocrine and solid pseudopapillary lesions.
Aspirations: tests sent per aspirate, specimen adequacy, non-diagnostic rate, post-procedure pancreatitis, and whether each result changed the recorded plan.
Molecular panels sent, result, decision taken on it, and final histology where an operation followed.

Progression events: new worrisome feature, new high-risk stigma, and pancreatic carcinoma, by schedule assigned and by time from enrolment, separating IPMN-derived from carcinoma arising elsewhere in the gland.
Stopping decisions by rule applied, with any pancreatic cancer diagnosed in a patient after surveillance was stopped reported as a named event.
Post-resection surveillance: schedule assigned by final histology and margin status, remnant recurrence, and reoperation.
Surveillance studies performed per year, by schedule and size band, against cancers and high-grade dysplasia detected.

approvals.q: Which guideline is this programme's spine — Kyoto 2024, ACG 2018, the European 2018 guideline, or AGA 2015?
approvals.why: NCCN takes no position and tells the reader to use the most recent available cyst guideline. The four differ on intervals, on resection thresholds and on stopping, and no study compares them. Until one is named, the same patient is managed differently depending on who sees them.
approvals.audit: Guideline and version recorded on every board output; proportion of cases managed off the named schedule.

approvals.q: Which surveillance interval schedule, stated by size band, and which modality?
approvals.why: The four schedules differ by a factor of three or more in imaging per patient-decade for the same cyst, and three of the four state in their own texts that their intervals are not evidence-based. A schedule assembled case by case cannot be audited and cannot generate a growth rate. The ACG 2 to 3 cm band is now resolved from the full text — MRI or EUS every 6 to 12 months for 3 years, then yearly for 4 — so the remaining question is which guideline, not which reading of a figure.
approvals.audit: Schedule assigned at enrolment; adherence to interval; proportion of scans on the assigned modality.

approvals.q: The stopping rule: continue while fit, stop at 5 years of stability, or stop by age and size?
approvals.why: Each has a different failure mode. Continuing indefinitely spends imaging on patients who will die of something else; stopping at 5 years accepts a documented 4.4% rate of invasive cancer after that point in one referral cohort; the age-and-size rule rests on two and three cancers with confidence intervals compatible with a threefold excess, in a retrospective cohort no guideline has endorsed. The three supporting cohorts differ in baseline selection, in conditioning on survival to 5 years, in whether high-grade dysplasia counts as an event against an invasive-cancer comparator, and in how long they watched past the mark — and those four differences account for their opposite conclusions. Choosing a rule means choosing one of those designs.
approvals.audit: Stopping decisions by rule applied, and any pancreatic cancer diagnosed after surveillance stopped, reported as a named event.

approvals.q: Does a cyst of 30 mm, or 40 mm, trigger resection on size alone in a fit patient?
approvals.why: Sendai 2006 made more than 30 mm a resection trigger from multivariate analyses in two series of 15 and 32 patients; Fukuoka 2012 demoted size on the ground that it is a weaker indicator than nodules or cytology; Fukuoka 2017 said size alone is not an appropriate parameter to indicate surgery while keeping 3 cm as a worrisome feature and 2 cm as a consideration under 65; Kyoto 2024 keeps it as a worrisome feature; the European guideline makes 40 mm a relative indication. A single worrisome feature carried a non-significant hazard ratio in the validation cohort, and that same cohort found risk stratified at 20 mm but not at 30 mm. The evidence does not support size alone — but the European position is live and is held by serious people.
approvals.audit: Resections by largest cyst dimension and by number of worrisome features, with final histology.

approvals.q: Mucinous cystic neoplasm: resect all in fit patients, or surveil those under 40 mm without risk features?
approvals.why: NCCN, summarising the international group, says resect all; the European evidence-based guideline says it is safe to follow those under 40 mm. The malignant risk is under 15%, and the two positions differ by a substantial number of distal pancreatectomies a year.
approvals.audit: Mucinous cystic neoplasms by size, management chosen, and final histology in every resected case.

approvals.q: Cyst fluid panel: does glucose replace CEA as first-line, is cytology mandatory on every aspirate, and is molecular testing offered and funded?
approvals.why: Glucose outperformed CEA head to head on pooled data, but neither ACG nor the European guideline names it, Kyoto quotes it without recommending it, and the two meta-analyses behind it pool largely the same seven primary studies so are not independent confirmation of each other. The molecular panel has good prospective multi-institutional data, is required by no guideline, is a single laboratory's assay analysed in a single laboratory, has a coverage question, and has a sensitivity of 47% rather than 90% for mucinous cystic neoplasm specifically. [PAYER]
approvals.audit: Tests sent per aspirate, non-diagnostic rate, and whether each result changed the recorded plan.

approvals.q: Is endoscopic ultrasound required before every cyst resection, or selectively?
approvals.why: Kyoto 2024 says aspiration should not be done when a high-risk stigma is obvious and surgery will follow regardless; ACG makes EUS conditional on specific triggers. A standing EUS costs a procedure in every case; a selective policy accepts that some resections are decided on cross-sectional imaging alone, in a disease where one diagnosis in four turns out to be wrong.
approvals.audit: Proportion of cyst resections with preoperative EUS, and the final histology in each.

approvals.q: How is growth defined — and is duct growth recorded as well as cyst growth?
approvals.why: There are four definitions, not three: Kyoto 2.5 mm per year, ACG more than 3 mm per year, Fukuoka 2017 5 mm over 2 years, the European guideline 5 mm per year. Kyoto adopted 2.5 because it was the value most frequently reported among candidates spanning 0.96 to 3.5 mm per year, which is a choice by vote frequency rather than performance. None has published measurement reproducibility and 2.5 mm is inside the range over which two readers can disagree. Separately, in the one cohort that measured both, the increase in main pancreatic duct diameter over 5 years predicted later carcinoma (SHR 1.71 per mm, 1.44 to 2.03) and the increase in cyst size did not (1.46, 0.96 to 2.20) — and no guideline records duct growth, Kyoto having considered and rejected it for lack of evidence.
approvals.audit: Report completeness for size and duct diameter; proportion of progression events declared on a same-modality comparison.

approvals.q: What happens to high-grade dysplasia at the duct margin when clearing it requires a total pancreatectomy?
approvals.why: Kyoto 2024 recommends additional resection for high-grade dysplasia at the frozen-section margin and, separately, permits leaving it. The full text conditions the permission on the patient being older or frail, on invasive cancer already being present so that prognosis is set by the invasive component, and on colloid-type disease. The unresolved case is high-grade dysplasia at the margin with no invasive component in a fit patient, where clearing it may mean a total pancreatectomy at 25% major morbidity and 6% 30-day mortality (95% CI 4 to 8%). This should not be settled for the first time in theatre. [EXPERTISE]
approvals.audit: Margin grade, extent taken, 90-day morbidity and mortality, and remnant recurrence.

approvals.q: Post-resection surveillance: which schedule, and is a resected non-invasive branch-duct IPMN with a clear margin followed at all?
approvals.why: Kyoto, ACG and the European guideline surveil every resected IPMN; AGA 2015 recommends against surveillance of resected cysts without high-grade dysplasia or malignancy and concedes that no case series report outcomes in that group. The best recurrence series found 9% recurrence after non-invasive IPMN, with 1 of 197 non-invasive branch-duct lesions (0.5%) recurring as cancer, and suggested surveillance could be avoided in selected cases — while the series Fukuoka 2017 cites found the 10-year risk of a new IPMN after resection of non-invasive disease to be 62%, with invasive IPMN in 38%. Decide also whether a resected mucinous cystic neoplasm without cancer is followed, where ACG says no on an absence of events in a 90-patient series and the European guideline is silent.
approvals.audit: Post-resection schedule assigned by histology, remnant recurrence, and reoperation.

approvals.q: Is there an age or fitness threshold for entering surveillance at all?
approvals.why: All four guidelines agree surveillance stops when a patient is no longer a surgical candidate, and AGA 2015 comes closest to an entry rule by calling surveillance inappropriate where life expectancy is limited, but none states one. Standardised incidence ratios suggest a stable small cyst adds nothing to background risk in patients over 75 — from 3 cancers, with an interval of 0.23 to 3.39 — and all-cause mortality in that group is about sixteen times disease-specific mortality. The ratio also falls with age because the comparator population's incidence rises, so the competing-risk argument is the sound one and the standardised-incidence-ratio argument is not. Setting an entry rule is a governance decision with no comparative evidence either way.
approvals.audit: New surveillance enrolments by age and cyst size, with the reason for enrolment recorded.

approvals.q: Who owns the cyst registry, the recall report and the annual review of this page against current guideline versions?
approvals.why: Every schedule here assumes the next scan happens, and the default failure mode of a surveillance programme is silence. Kyoto 2024, ACG 2018, the European 2018 guideline and NCCN all revise on different cycles, and this page is a first draft with no ratified roadmap behind it.
approvals.audit: Named owner, with the guideline edition and date recorded, an agreed update cycle, and a monthly overdue-by-name report.

approvals.q: The mural nodule threshold: 5 mm, as Kyoto retains it, or 10 mm, which its own commissioned review found discriminates far better?
approvals.why: Kyoto 2024 reports that a mural nodule alone carries an odds ratio of 1.19 to 3.16 in recent multivariable models, and that one EUS analysis gave a 10 mm nodule an odds ratio of 7.90 with a 67% probability of high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma against 2.93 and under 19% for a nodule of 5 to 10 mm. It discussed moving to 10 mm and kept 5 mm for lack of evidence strongly supporting the change. The 5 mm line was itself chosen by expert agreement in 2017 after three candidate heights performed similarly. This threshold separates an operation from an interval scan and it is the single most consequential unexamined number on the page. A programme that keeps 5 mm should do so knowingly.
approvals.audit: Resections by nodule height and enhancement, with final histology; proportion of EUS reports stating nodule height in millimetres.

approvals.q: Is the Kyoto 30 mm size band retained for the 6-monthly interval, given that its only large validation found no stratification at 30 mm?
approvals.why: In the 3,336-patient cohort that validated the rest of the revised criteria, the subdistribution hazard ratio for later pancreatic cancer was 2.07 (1.38 to 3.10) at 20 to 29 mm and 1.75 (1.00 to 3.08) at 30 mm or more. The band that triggers the most imaging is the band that did not separate, and 9.2% of that cohort had cysts of 30 mm or more, all of them already carrying a worrisome feature or high-risk stigma. Keeping the band is defensible on prudence; it is not supported by the validation.
approvals.audit: Surveillance studies per patient-year by size band, and progression events by size band.

approvals.q: Is a local 'suspicious' cytology treated as an absolute surgical indication here, and who reads it?
approvals.why: Kyoto 2024 makes suspicious or positive cytology a high-risk stigma and puts the absolute risk of high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma at 91 to 100% and 100% for those two readings. The same document puts the overall sensitivity of cyst fluid cytology at 28.7% (4.8 to 61.5%), and 59 to 60% of specimens were less than optimal or unsatisfactory for cytology in the two large molecular series. The result is decisive one way and nearly uninformative the other, and it now sits inside the risk classification, so the programme needs a named cytopathology arrangement and an agreed vocabulary before it acts on the word 'suspicious'.
approvals.audit: Cytology category reported per aspirate, specimen adequacy, decision taken, and final histology where an operation followed.

approvals.q: Will this programme record and publish its own 90-day mortality and major morbidity for cyst resection?
approvals.why: Sendai 2006, Fukuoka 2012, Fukuoka 2017, Kyoto 2024 and the European 2018 guideline quantify surgical mortality and morbidity nowhere in their texts, so every threshold in the spine of this page is stated with the risk of not operating in numbers and the risk of operating not stated at all. The published comparators are 2.1% mortality with 30% morbidity for cyst resection (ACG), 2% with 30% in centres of excellence against 6.6% across US pancreatic surgery in SEER (AGA), 30-day mortality 2.4% with 17.1% major morbidity in 164 resections generated by a surveillance cohort, and 6% with 25% for total pancreatectomy. Without a local figure the consent conversation uses somebody else's.
approvals.audit: Resections for cystic neoplasm by operation, with 90-day mortality and major morbidity, reported at least annually.

approvals.q: Is the cost of this programme tracked, and by whom?
approvals.why: Up to $3.6 million is spent per cancer detected in US cyst surveillance, with no appreciable change in cyst-related pancreatic adenocarcinoma mortality over two decades of rising expenditure, and the two published cost-effectiveness models give $171,143 and $20,096 per quality-adjusted life-year for different cysts, guidelines and eras. No guideline in the IAP line and neither the European guideline nor ACG attempts a cost analysis, and ACG and AGA both state that none exists. This is not a reason to under-image anyone; it is a reason to know what the schedule chosen at item 2 commits the service to before it is chosen.
approvals.audit: Surveillance studies performed per year, by schedule and size band, with cancers and high-grade dysplasia detected.

approvals.q: Which cysts are formally released, and in writing — serous cystadenoma, pseudocyst, resected mucinous cystic neoplasm without cancer?
approvals.why: ACG makes three strong recommendations for discharge: no follow-up after resection of a serous cystadenoma, pseudocyst or other benign cyst, none after a resected mucinous cystic neoplasm without cancer, and the European guideline releases a radiologically confident serous cystadenoma after one year to symptom-based follow-up only. The strong recommendation for mucinous cystic neoplasm rests on an absence of events in a 90-patient series and a 344-case review. Against that, ACG asks for yearly follow-up for at least 5 years after resection of a solid pseudopapillary neoplasm, on a 4.4% recurrence rate at a median of 50.5 months, which this page previously omitted. Leaving benign lesions on a surveillance list is the clearest avoidable waste in the pathway; discharging the wrong one is not recoverable.
approvals.audit: Patients formally discharged by entity and reason, and any later presentation of a discharged lesion reported as a named event.

approvals.q: Which non-guideline adjuncts are offered — and is the page's own evidence summary reviewed when they are proposed?
approvals.why: Through-the-needle microforceps biopsy is in none of the four guidelines, its superiority claim over aspiration rests on two retrospective within-patient comparisons with an odds ratio spanning 1.12 to 67.12, and the meta-analysis's own results text states there was no significant difference in accuracy — contradicting its abstract. Needle-based confocal laser endomicroscopy is recommended against by the European guideline at GRADE 1C, and in the best training study trained readers reached only 57% sensitivity for mucinous cystic neoplasm and 65% for serous cystadenoma with interobserver agreement of kappa 0.32 and 0.44, which undercuts the economic case for it. Endoscopic ablation resolves cysts in 33 to 79% with adverse events in about 12%, has produced an adenocarcinoma after treatment, does not remove the need for surveillance, and Kyoto 2024 says it should only be performed in a clinical trial. If any of these is offered here it needs an indication, a consent form and a registry.
approvals.audit: Use of each adjunct by indication, adverse events, whether the result changed the plan, and final histology where an operation followed.

provenance: Revised on 7 October 2026 after a full-text read of the whole 27-paper reference depot for this page, with each paper abstracted to its results, the authors' stated limitations and an independent critique. The first draft had been built from abstracts and guideline summaries; four of the five documents that set the thresholds on this page — the international evidence-based Kyoto guidelines (Ohtsuka 2024, PMID 38182527), Fukuoka 2017 (PMID 28735806), Fukuoka 2012 (PMID 22687371) and the original Sendai consensus (PMID 16327281) — had not previously been checked against in full, and reading them changed the page's spine rather than its structure. What changed most: Kyoto 2024's malignancy rates of 31% and 62% are prevalences in resected specimens and the document itself now states that the real rate across all branch-duct IPMNs is much lower without quantifying it, so neither figure appears on this page as a surveillance risk; Kyoto retained the 5 mm mural nodule and 10 mm main-duct thresholds in the same passage that reports odds ratios of 1.19 to 3.16 and 1.06 to 1.76 for them and an odds ratio of 7.90 for a 10 mm nodule; the 2.5 mm per year growth threshold was adopted because 2.5 was the value reported most frequently among candidates spanning 0.96 to 3.5; no sensitivity, specificity or predictive value is published for any risk tier three guideline generations in; surgical mortality and cost-effectiveness appear nowhere in the IAP line of guidelines or the European guideline, so those numbers have been assembled from ACG, AGA, PROPAN and the surgical series; the only large external validation found that the 30 mm threshold did not stratify risk (subdistribution hazard ratio 1.75, 95% CI 1.00 to 3.08, against 2.07, 1.38 to 3.10, at 20 to 29 mm); and the three cohorts behind the stopping debate are shown on gate 9 to differ in baseline selection, in conditioning on survival to 5 years, in whether high-grade dysplasia is counted as an event against an invasive-cancer-only comparator, and in how long they observed past the 5-year mark, which accounts for their opposite conclusions. Two numbers flagged in the first draft as needing verification are now resolved from the full texts: the ACG 2 to 3 cm surveillance band is MRI or EUS every 6 to 12 months for 3 years then yearly for 4, and the Kyoto cyst-fluid glucose threshold is 50 mg/dL with 93% sensitivity and 89% specificity. Three claims in the first draft were wrong and have been corrected: Kyoto does quantify needle-tract and peritoneal seeding (0.3%, and 2.3% against 4.4%, P=0.403); Kyoto and the European guideline do give operating characteristics for serum CA 19-9; and the European guideline does not merely omit needle-based confocal laser endomicroscopy from its algorithm but recommends against it at GRADE 1C. Grades were lowered where the full text showed a threshold to be a consensus value rather than a derived one, and the reason is stated in each note. The current narrative review of the field (Gardner 2024, PMID 38442782) is cited only for its cost figures, its population-versus-individual framing and its list of circumstances in which stopping is uncontroversial: its table of branch-duct transformation rates pools structurally incompatible denominators into an apparent 3.5 to 5.5% agreement, and its guideline-comparison table misreports several criteria, so no rate and no criterion on this page comes from it. Three sources on this page were not in the depot and are not full-text verified to the same standard: NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma Version 1.2026, from the extracted text supplied to the programme with its Discussion dated 6 August 2026, which has no cyst algorithm of its own, cites Kyoto 2024 as the international standard, cites the superseded 2013 European consensus statement rather than the 2018 evidence-based guideline, and directs the reader to the most recent available guideline; the 2013 European consensus statement itself (PMID 23415799), cited from its PubMed record only and listed because it is the document NCCN reaches for; and the WHO 5th edition entity definitions, used but not re-verified against the current online edition. This is a first draft and there is no ratified roadmap behind it. Unlike the programme's five existing disease roadmaps, this pathway transcribes no approved institutional document — there is no local pancreatic cyst protocol in the source set — and it takes no institutional position of its own. Where the four guidelines disagree, which on this disease is on almost everything that matters, the page shows the disagreement and refers the choice to the nineteen ratification items in the approvals section; the order of options in any gate reflects guideline standing or the spine chosen for this page, never a demonstrated advantage. It is not active clinical policy, it does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use.
